steps.notes: allowed_orders: depletable iff resource is current top-available for >=1 species. Literal impl matches all 3 targets (full 6-perm set, single, 2-perm subset), all in itertools lex order.
G_mat: G[i,j]=g[i, top pref of species i not in first j depleted]. Matches all 3 targets; outputs are exactly the G matrices hard-coded as inputs in 56.3 -> internally consistent.

check_G_feasibility: solve G t = log(D)*1, feasible iff unique solution with all t>0. Matches False/True/False. D-independence (background) holds. Test sign margins are large; t>0 vs t>=0 boundary never exercised.

get_dep_orders: compose 56.1+56.2+56.3. Matches [[2,1,3]],[[3,1,4,2]],[]. Iterating ALL perms+feasibility gives identical results to allowed+feasibility (allowed pre-filter not load-bearing on these cases); no singular-matrix crashes.

overall_assessment: Problem 56 is fair to score as-is. Dependencies (itertools, numpy, math) import cleanly on numpy 2.2.6 / scipy 1.15.2 (no D12). All four steps are fully specified and internally consistent: 56.2's outputs are byte-for-byte the G matrices fed into 56.3, and a literal expert implementation passes all 12 test cases under official joint scoring. Two latent fragilities were examined and judged non-defects: (1) steps 56.1/56.4 return an order-unspecified 'list of tuples' compared with order-sensitive np.allclose, but every frozen target is in canonical itertools.permutations lexicographic order, which the explicitly-imported itertools and the 'R! orders then filter' phrasing strongly imply, so a competent solver matches; the 56.4 targets are singletons/empty where order is moot anyway. (2) 56.4's feasibility-over-all-permutations equals allowed-then-feasibility for all three cases, so the optional 'allowed' pre-filter cannot cause a false positive. Tests are discriminating (neither constant-True nor constant-False passes 56.3; 'return all permutations' fails 56.1; empty-only fails 56.4). No defects that would mis-score a competent solver.
